À la rentrée des classes, si la pandémie: As the new school year begins, the pandemic is raising fears, but hundreds of children in Quebec dread something else: the return of bullying at school.What do you do when you learn that your 7-year-old is talking about suicide at school? That he suffered a head injury from repeated blows by his classmates? That you have to pick him up morning, noon and night so he doesn’t become a target of violence?
C’est ce qu’a fait Khadija Barbe, qui vo: That’s what Khadija Barbe has done. She has watched her son buckle under the blows of bullying at school for more than a year. “I’m at the end of my rope. We’re asking for a change of school, but once again I keep hitting walls,” says little Samy’s mother. For months, she says, she has been stuck in an endless bureaucratic maze, with her son in distress at the centre of it all. “Right from mid-September, we knew he was being hit at school. He didn’t talk about it, but he often came home with marks and injuries, and with no incident report. We also noticed a change in his behaviour, and restless sleep.”
Suite à ces constats et quelques comment: Following these observations and a few comments from the teacher, the mother decided to have her son assessed by a neuropsychologist. Several diagnoses came out of it, including ADHD and an anxiety disorder. These were added to other disorders identified earlier, notably with language and vision. All these differences make him an easy target, believes Samy’s mother. “I had already noticed some violent behaviour toward my son last year, for example when I accompanied the class on a field trip. But I always gave them the benefit of the doubt. You don’t want to believe your child is being bullied.”
Aujourd’hui, elle n’a plus de doute. Ell: Today, she no longer has any doubt. She also asked the CLSC for help, and it went to the schoolyard to document the shoving incidents involving her son. The child’s family doctor also identified a head injury and recommended that the child be moved to a different class.
Cette demande est refusée par l’école et: The school refused this request and, according to Ms. Barbe, the incidents continue to be downplayed. Despite an intervention plan, the violence continues and little Samy is not believed when he reports the injustices he is suffering. In a letter sent to parents by school staff, the school even confirmed that it was “not trying to find out who throws the first punch,” inviting all the parents involved to talk with their children about their behaviour. “That letter was the last straw! How can anyone claim to want to resolve a situation without trying to find out who throws the first punch, who is defending themselves and who is provoking?” the mother laments.Contacted for comment on this article, the school and the school board declined an interview request. They did assure us, however, that: “The school administration and the general management of the Centre de services scolaire have taken the situation very seriously.
Conformément au code de vie de l’école e: In accordance with the school’s code of conduct and the Plan to Combat Bullying and Violence, and following close communication with the parent, measures have been put in place to resolve the situation. Like all schools in Quebec, it is important to point out that every school in the Centre de services scolaire des Mille-Îles has a Plan to Combat Bullying and Violence.”
Le problème, pour la mère de Samy, c’est: The problem, for Samy’s mother, is that this battle for her son’s well-being has almost become a full-time job. On top of having to pick him up morning, noon and night at school, she is constantly involved in proceedings, whether with the police and Youth Protection (DPJ), both of which she contacted herself, the school board, the student ombudsman, health professionals, and more. “The CLSC doesn’t want to get on the school’s bad side, the police don’t get involved, the MNAs can’t do anything....
Il est là le problème! C’est pour ça que: That’s the problem! That’s why it keeps going and will keep going for a long time, because nobody wants to stick their neck out and take concrete action!” says the exasperated mother.Debra J. Peppler, a psychologist who is an expert in bullying and violence and a professor at York University in Ontario, is not surprised. “It’s a reality we see a lot. Parents have no choice but to fight for their children’s well-being. In Ontario, several situations even end up in court, but most are settled out of court, so we don’t have access to that case law to advance the cause.” In Quebec, a first trial pitting a family whose child was bullied against a school board concluded in 2018.
La famille a eu gain de cause, prouvant: The family won, proving that the school had not done enough to protect their daughter. Since 2011, following the suicide of a teenage girl, the Quebec government has had a law to act against bullying and violence in schools. Among other things, the law requires schools to adopt an action plan that must set out how to prevent bullying, report cases, ensure the confidentiality of complaints, act when a case is reported, and support victims and witnesses. Students must also receive training on bullying and know what sanctions may apply. The plan to combat violence and bullying must also provide for consequences for students who engage in this kind of behaviour. “The plan was drawn up with the help of experts in childhood, and current research indicates that ‘punishing’ bullies is not necessarily always the best approach.
On travaillera idéalement plutôt en prév: Ideally, we’ll work instead on prevention and repair, but obviously every case is unique,” says Jean-François Rioux, secretary general of the Fédération des comités de parents du Québec.
Dr Peppler est d’accord. « Ce qu’il faut: Dr. Peppler agrees. “What you have to understand is that a child who bullies is often a victim of some form of bullying themselves, often at home. They then use the concept of a power hierarchy to their advantage,” she explains. “And by imposing a suspension or a punishment, what does the child learn? That whoever is in a position of power (the adult) can impose their will. It’s better to work on offering an opportunity for repair and positive leadership (going to help younger children in a kindergarten class, for example).The impact of this law is also hard to measure, since there is currently no mechanism to assess its reach. “Every year, schools still write an annual report to take stock of the situation and collect data. Schools are also encouraged to review the plan every year to update it in light of how things have evolved,” says Jean-François Rioux.
Debra Peppler se désole tout de même que: Debra Peppler nonetheless laments that Canada has not adopted a national plan to fight bullying, as many other countries did long ago. According to a study conducted by the WHO, Canada ranks 26th and 27th out of 35 countries when it comes to fighting bullying in schools. That is why the psychologist is working with the Prevnet team to create a national network to combat violence and bullying.
Leur but : créer des ponts entre la scie: Their goal: to build bridges between science, research and the people on the ground who work with children. Their website offers resources and a “toolbox” that details the steps to follow when a problem arises. Little Samy is not the only one living the hell of bullying as early as elementary school. A 2017 survey by Université Laval’s Research Chair on Well-being at School and Violence Prevention shows that 15% of Quebec students (160,000 children) experience recurring violence (more than three times a month) at school.This violence has lasting consequences. Researchers from Lancaster University, the University of Wollongong and the University of Sydney revealed at the Royal Economic Society’s annual conference that having been bullied at school increased the risk of mental illness at age 25 by 40% and raised the risk of being unemployed at age 25 by about 35%. Another longitudinal study in Britain followed bullied children from around age 10 to age 50.
Le constat est sans équivoque : les effe: The finding is unequivocal: the effects of this violence can last for decades.
«Écoutez les enfants. Ils savent mieux q: “Listen to children. They know better than we do what’s going on. They have fundamental human rights, and those rights are being trampled,” concludes Dr. Peppler.

Communiquez avec le directeur de l’école: Contact the school principal so that an effective intervention is carried out with your child and the aggressor, in accordance with the school’s plan to combat bullying and violence.
Si votre enfant présente des symptômes a: If your child has symptoms affecting their physical and mental health, have them assessed by the family doctor or another relevant expert. Keep written records of these steps.
Si vous n’avez pas de nouvelles, communi: If you don’t hear back, contact the school principal again, this time in writing (email or letter), sending a copy to the general management of the school service centre (CSS).
Si vous êtes toujours insatisfaits, vous: If you are still dissatisfied, you can also contact the designated student ombudsman of the CSS or school board. <l1>The student ombudsman</l1> is meant to act as a mediator at the end of the process when the complainant is dissatisfied with the review of their complaint.
Si vous jugez que la sécurité de votre e: If you believe your child’s safety is threatened, don’t hesitate to contact the police.
Ce recours vous appartient, peu importe: This option is yours regardless of what steps the school has taken.
